sentence: Replication keeps a copy of the same data on multiple machines connected via a network.
Partitioning splits a large dataset into smaller subsets assigned to different nodes.
The system sustained a throughput of 10,000 requests per second under load.
Retrying an idempotent operation is safe because applying it twice has the same effect as once.
Tail latency matters more than the average when users issue many requests per page.
The single leader became a bottleneck once write volume doubled.
Document databases let you write data without first declaring a schema.
If any statement fails, the database performs a rollback of the whole transaction.
A cache stores the result of an expensive computation for faster reads later.
Denormalization duplicates data to avoid expensive joins at read time.
Automatic failover promotes a follower to leader when the old leader dies.
Backpressure lets a slow consumer signal the producer to stop sending so fast.
As we saw in Chapter 5, a quorum protects reads from stale replicas.
Compaction was covered in detail in Chapter 3, where SSTables merge in the background.
See Chapter 7 for why serializability is the strongest isolation level.
Chapter 6 describes rebalancing, the process of moving partitions between nodes.
We will define linearizability precisely in Chapter 9; for now think of it as single-copy behavior.
Recall the hinted handoff mechanism introduced in Chapter 5 for sloppy quorums.
Two-phase commit, which Chapter 9 examines closely, coordinates atomic commits across nodes.
Chapter 11 turns to stream processing, where inputs are unbounded and arrive over time.
As we discussed earlier, write amplification is one effect of repeated compaction.
Read repair, mentioned before, fixes stale values during reads.
Earlier we discussed split brain, where two nodes both believe they are the leader.
Leader election, covered earlier in this book, decides which replica accepts writes.
We touched on skew earlier — some partitions receive far more load than others.
ZooKeeper stores membership in ephemeral nodes that vanish when a session ends.
A monotonic clock always moves forward, unlike a time-of-day clock.
A byzantine fault means a node may behave arbitrarily, even maliciously.
